title: Alphabet takes its AI debt spree Down Under with a first Australian dollar bond
excerpt: Alphabet is preparing its first-ever Australian dollar bond, an inaugural ‘Kangaroo’ deal of about US$3.6bn (roughly A$5bn) to help fund its AI build-out.
content_html:
Alphabet is preparing to sell its first bond denominated in Australian dollars, a modest-sounding piece of financial housekeeping that says a good deal about how the AI build-out is now being paid for.

According to bookrunner messages reported by Reuters, the Google parent has hired ANZ, Deutsche Bank, RBC Capital Markets, and TD Securities to arrange an inaugural “Kangaroo” deal, the market’s shorthand for a foreign borrower issuing in Aussie dollars.

The structure is unshowy but telling. Alphabet is weighing four tranches, at three, five, ten, and twenty years, with the shorter two offered as either fixed or floating and the longer pair fixed only.

That is the maturity spread of a borrower planning to be a repeat visitor rather than a one-off tourist, laddering its debts so that not everything comes due at once. Pricing guidance could land as early as Tuesday, with the deal itself following a day later.

The reason for all this is no mystery. Only weeks ago Alphabet raised US$25bn in a twice-yearly dollar bond to bankroll its AI expansion, and in June it topped that up with an equity raise of around $85bn.

The Australian trip is the same story told in a different accent: a company that has lifted its 2026 capital-expenditure guidance by $15bn, to somewhere between $195bn and $205bn, casting about for every pool of capital it can reasonably reach.

Why bother with a market a fraction the size of New York’s?

Partly because it is there, and increasingly fashionable. Kangaroo issuance has hit a record of about A$60bn this year, some 40% above 2025, as the world’s largest borrowers hunt for buyers beyond the dollar.

Alphabet has been doing precisely that, having also lined up a debut yen bond earlier in the same funding spree. Spreading the borrowing across currencies widens the investor base and, with a following wind, shaves a few basis points off the cost.

There is a symbolic dimension too. “Not only is it Alphabet’s first-ever Australian dollar bond, but it’s also the first AI hyperscaler to access the Australian dollar market,” noted Chamath De Silva of BetaShares, and the deal would comfortably eclipse the roughly $2.25bn Apple sold in Australia more than a decade ago.

The country’s pension funds, flush with the compulsory retirement savings that Australians are obliged to set aside and forever short of high-grade paper to put them in, make a natural home for a top-rated borrower’s debt.

The wrinkle, and there is always a wrinkle, is what the borrowing says about the economics underneath it. Alphabet posted its first negative quarterly free cash flow as a public company in the second quarter, around negative $5.9bn, as the cost of chips, data centres, and power outran even its formidable cash generation.

That is the pattern across the sector, where Big Tech’s AI spending is catching up with its cash flow, and the industry is expected to lay out north of $730bn this year, much of it on artificial intelligence.

Which is how the most cash-rich companies in history have quietly turned into some of its most enthusiastic borrowers. Big Tech’s AI debt has swelled past $350bn and gone shopping across Europe and Asia for willing lenders, a striking turn for firms that once treated debt as an admission of weakness.

The Australian bond is a small chapter in that larger book, but a revealing one. When a company perched on a mountain of cash starts raising money in a currency it has never touched before.

Yet, the interesting question is not whether investors will buy, they will, but what the appetite tells us about a spending race that nobody has yet worked out how to stop.

content_html_zh:
Alphabet 正准备出售其第一笔以澳元计价的债券，这是一项听起来温和的金融管理举措，充分说明了人工智能建设目前是如何支付费用的。

据路透社报道的账簿管理人消息，谷歌母公司已聘请澳新银行、德意志银行、加拿大皇家银行资本市场和道明证券安排首笔“袋鼠”交易，这是市场对外国借款人以澳元发行债券的简写。

结构并不显眼，但却很能说明问题。 Alphabet 正在权衡四档，分别为三年、五年、十年和二十年，其中较短的两档以固定或浮动的形式提供，而较长的两档则仅固定。

这是计划成为回头客而不是一次性游客的借款人的到期利差，其债务逐步增加，这样就不会立即到期所有债务。 定价指导最早可能在周二出台，交易本身将在一天后公布。

这一切的原因并不神秘。 就在几周前，Alphabet 通过每年两次的美元债券筹集了 250 亿美元，为其人工智能扩张提供资金，6 月份，该公司又筹集了约 850 亿美元的股票，以补充这一资金。

这次澳大利亚之行以不同的口音讲述了同样的故事：这家公司将 2026 年资本支出指引提高了 150 亿美元，达到 1950 亿美元至 2050 亿美元之间，为它可以合理达到的所有资本池进行投资。

为什么要为一个只有纽约市场规模一小部分的市场而烦恼呢？

部分原因是它的存在，而且越来越时尚。 随着全球最大的借款人寻找美元以外的买家，袋鼠发行量今年已创下约 600 亿澳元的记录，比 2025 年增长约 40%。

Alphabet 正是这样做的，在同一轮融资热潮中，Alphabet 早些时候还发行了首次发行的日元债券。 将借贷分散到不同货币可以扩大投资者基础，并在紧随其后的推动下，将成本削减几个基点。

还有一个象征意义的维度。 BetaShares 的查马斯·德席尔瓦 (Chamath De Silva) 表示：“这不仅是 Alphabet 有史以来第一只澳元债券，也是第一只进入澳元市场的人工智能超大规模债券。”这笔交易将轻松超越苹果十多年前在澳大利亚出售的约 22.5 亿美元。

该国的养老基金充满了澳大利亚人必须留出的强制性退休储蓄，而且永远缺乏高级票据来存放这些储蓄，因此成为了顶级借款人债务的天然家园。

皱纹，而且总是有皱纹，就是借款所反映的其背后的经济学。 Alphabet 在第二季度首次公布了作为上市公司的负季度自由现金流，约为负 59 亿美元，因为芯片、数据中心和电力的成本甚至超过了其强大的现金产生能力。

这就是整个行业的模式，大型科技公司的人工智能支出正在赶上其现金流，预计该行业今年的投资将超过 7300 亿美元，其中大部分用于人工智能。

这就是历史上现金最充裕的公司如何悄然变成最热情的借款人的原因。 大型科技公司的人工智能债务已突破 3500 亿美元，并在欧洲和亚洲寻找愿意贷款的人，这对于那些曾经将债务视为承认弱点的公司来说是一个惊人的转变。

澳大利亚债券只是这本书中的一小章，但却具有启发意义。 当一家拥有大量现金的公司开始以从未接触过的货币筹集资金时。

然而，有趣的问题不是投资者是否会购买，而是他们会购买，而是胃口告诉我们关于一场尚未有人找到如何阻止的消费竞赛的信息。
